package.pinned_comment: Do your freckles fade in winter, or do they stick around all year?
package.script: You were born with zero freckles. Not a single one. They usually start showing up around age two. Then some kids get a few, while others end up with hundreds. So why do some people get way more freckles than others? First, what is a freckle, really? Your skin gets its color from a pigment called melanin. It's made by special cells called melanocytes, tucked deep in the bottom layer of your skin. Each one pumps out tiny packets of pigment, and hands them to the skin cells around it. Here's the surprise. A freckle doesn't have extra pigment cells. It has about the same number as the skin next to it. Those cells are just working way harder, making a lot more melanin in one tiny spot. Most freckles are smaller than three millimeters. And they show up most on fair skin, which has less melanin to begin with. So what makes those cells work overtime? Sunlight. When ultraviolet light hits your skin, it switches your melanocytes into high gear. Melanin is your body's sunshade. It soaks up UV light before it can damage your DNA. In most skin, that extra melanin spreads out evenly, and you get a tan. But in freckly skin, it piles up in little patches. That's why freckles darken every summer, and fade, or even disappear, in winter. And it's why babies, who've barely seen the sun, don't have any yet. But two kids can play in the same sun, and only one ends up covered in freckles. That's where your genes come in. The big one is a gene called MC1R. Think of it as a switch on every melanocyte. When it works normally, the cell makes eumelanin, a dark brown pigment that's great at blocking sun. But scientists have found more than 80 versions of MC1R. And some of them are ancient. One may date back around 80,000 years. Some of them flip the switch toward pheomelanin instead, a reddish yellow pigment that protects much less. Those same versions are behind red hair. Most redheads carry two of them, and almost all carry at least one. That's why red hair and freckles so often go together. Still, one copy doesn't guarantee freckles. Some people without these versions freckle anyway, because lots of other genes play a part too. Now, not every brown spot is a freckle. Doctors call real freckles ephelides. Real freckles come and go with the seasons, and many fade as you get older. Sun spots, or solar lentigines, are different. They're larger, they show up in middle age, after years of sun, and they stay put all winter long. Under a microscope, sun spots really do have extra pigment cells. So what do freckles tell you? Freckly skin usually makes less of that protective brown melanin, so it burns more easily. That's why skin doctors tell freckly people, to be extra careful with sunscreen. So freckles aren't random dots. They're tiny patches of sunshade, switched on extra hard, mostly thanks to one tiny gene. Next up, how do your lungs breathe, more than 20,000 times a day?
key_facts: Freckles are rare on infants and commonly first appear around age 2 (Medscape)
Freckles have about the same number of melanocytes as nearby skin; the cells make more melanin (Wikipedia, DermNet, Medscape)
UV light increases melanin production; freckles darken in summer and fade in winter (DermNet)
Ephelides are usually under 3 mm across (DermNet)
More than 80 MC1R variants have been identified (Helix); some MC1R variants linked to freckling and red hair, one (Arg160Trp) estimated ~80,000 years old (Wikipedia)
Most redheads have two MC1R variants and almost all have one (Wikipedia)
Solar lentigines are larger, appear in middle age, persist in winter and have more melanocytes (DermNet, Medscape)
Freckly skin has less photo-protective melanin and is more susceptible to UV damage (Wikipedia)

Lobsters never stop growing.

package.script: Snakes never choke on meals wider than their own heads. Your jaw could never. So how? First, a myth. Snakes don't unhinge their jaws. Hippos sweat bright red, but not blood.
How do they never get sunburned when you would?
Hippos spend their days soaking in African rivers,
but they often haul out onto sunny banks,
and their skin has a super thin outer layer
that dries out fast.
So it oozes a thick, oily goo.
At first it's clear.
Then, within minutes,
it turns bright red,
and later, brown.
People call it blood sweat,
but it's not blood,
and it's not really sweat either.

one red and one orange.

like built-in sunscreen.

so scrapes from hippo fights stay cleaner.

in one gooey coat.

package.title: How Do Your Lungs Breathe 20,000 Times a Day?
package.description:
How do your lungs work? Your lungs can't breathe on their own: the diaphragm pulls air down a branching airway tree into about 480 million alveoli, where oxygen swaps into your blood and carbon dioxide comes out.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/52250-lung.html
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_alveolus
https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/lung-and-airway-disorders/biology-of-the-lungs-and-airways/control-of-breathing

package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think your lungs did the pulling, or the diaphragm? 🫁
package.script:
Your lungs can't breathe on their own,
yet you breathe more than 20,000 times a day,
without ever thinking about it.
So what's really pulling the air in?
And what happens to it once it's inside?
Let's follow one breath, all the way in.
First, the engine.
And it isn't your lungs.
It's a muscle underneath them, called the diaphragm,
a dome shaped like an upside-down bowl.
When you breathe in, it tightens and pulls down flat.
Your ribs swing up and out at the same time.
Your chest gets bigger,
so the air pressure inside drops,
and outside air rushes in to fill the space.
Your lungs just stretch along, like balloons in a box.
Breathing out at rest is even easier.
The diaphragm relaxes,
and your stretchy lungs spring back like a rubber band,
pushing the air out.
Each calm breath moves about half a liter.
Over a whole day, that's roughly 10,000 liters of air.
Now let's follow that air inside.
It goes down your windpipe, the trachea,
which splits into two tubes, one for each lung.
Then those tubes split again, and again,
about 23 times,
into thinner and thinner branches.
Doctors call it the bronchial tree,
because it looks like a tree growing upside down.
Lay every tube end to end,
and by one estimate, they'd stretch about 2,400 kilometers.
The tubes are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs called cilia.
They trap dust and germs,
and sweep them back up toward your throat,
where you swallow them without noticing.
And your lungs aren't twins.
The right one has three sections, called lobes.
The left one has only two,
because it leaves room for your heart.
Now here's where the magic happens.
At the end of every tiny branch,
there's a bunch of air sacs, like grapes.
They're called alveoli.
And you've got around 480 million of them.
Each one is wrapped in a net of tiny blood vessels.
The wall between the air and your blood,
is about 200 times thinner than a sheet of paper.
So oxygen just slips across, into your blood.
At the same time, carbon dioxide, your body's waste gas,
slips the other way, into the air sac,
ready to be breathed out.
Spread all those sacs out flat,
and they'd cover about 70 square meters.
That's roughly a badminton court,
folded up inside your chest.
So who's in charge of all this?
Not you, most of the time.
A spot in your brainstem runs breathing on autopilot.
And here's the surprise.
It mostly isn't watching your oxygen.
It's watching carbon dioxide.
When CO2 builds up in your blood,
your brainstem tells the diaphragm to breathe faster.
That burning need to breathe when you hold your breath?
That's mostly carbon dioxide piling up, not oxygen running out.
In fact, the air you breathe out still has about 16 percent oxygen,
compared to 21 percent going in.
So your lungs aren't really pumps.
They're a giant, folded-up trading floor,
where air and blood swap gases,
over 20,000 times a day, every day of your life.
Next up, why can some animals see colors,
we can't even imagine?
key_facts: The lungs have no muscle to inflate themselves; the diaphragm and rib muscles enlarge the chest, pressure drops and air flows in
Quiet exhalation is mostly passive elastic recoil
A resting breath is about 0.5 L; roughly 20,000 breaths a day
Airways branch about 23 times (bronchial tree); one estimate puts total airway length near 2,400 km
Right lung has 3 lobes, left has 2 (cardiac notch)
About 480 million alveoli, about 70 square meters of surface
The blood-air barrier is well under a micrometer thick
The brainstem drives breathing mainly from CO2 levels
Exhaled air still holds about 16% oxygen vs about 21% inhaled

Your ribs swing up and out at the same time.

13
00:00:28,380 --> 00:00:29,520
Your chest gets bigger,

14
00:00:29,850 --> 00:00:31,720
so the air pressure inside drops,

15
00:00:32,040 --> 00:00:34,460
and outside air rushes in to fill the space.

16
00:00:34,860 --> 00:00:37,950
Your lungs just stretch along, like balloons in a box.

17
00:00:38,310 --> 00:00:40,280
Breathing out at rest is even easier.

18
00:00:40,630 --> 00:00:42,000
The diaphragm relaxes,

19
00:00:42,360 --> 00:00:44,910
and your stretchy lungs spring back like a rubber band,

20
00:00:45,230 --> 00:00:46,200
pushing the air out.

21
00:00:46,680 --> 00:00:48,860
Each calm breath moves about half a liter.

22
00:00:49,250 --> 00:00:52,430
Over a whole day, that's roughly 10,000 liters of air.

23
00:00:52,800 --> 00:00:54,520
Now let's follow that air inside.

24
00:00:54,930 --> 00:00:57,130
It goes down your windpipe, the trachea,

25
00:00:57,290 --> 00:01:00,040
which splits into two tubes, one for each lung.

26
00:01:00,420 --> 00:01:02,770
Then those tubes split again, and again,

27
00:01:03,030 --> 00:01:04,300
about 23 times,

28
00:01:04,370 --> 00:01:06,030
into thinner and thinner branches.

29
00:01:06,470 --> 00:01:08,260
Doctors call it the bronchial tree,

30
00:01:08,650 --> 00:01:11,030
because it looks like a tree growing upside down.

31
00:01:11,400 --> 00:01:12,900
Lay every tube end to end,

32
00:01:13,280 --> 00:01:17,780
and by one estimate, they'd stretch about 2,400 kilometers.

33
00:01:18,180 --> 00:01:21,830
The tubes are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs called cilia.

34
00:01:22,180 --> 00:01:23,730
They trap dust and germs,

35
00:01:24,050 --> 00:01:25,780
and sweep them back up toward your throat,

36
00:01:26,140 --> 00:01:27,800
where you swallow them without noticing.

37
00:01:28,150 --> 00:01:29,510
And your lungs aren't twins.

38
00:01:29,960 --> 00:01:32,350
The right one has three sections, called lobes.

39
00:01:32,750 --> 00:01:34,020
The left one has only two,

40
00:01:34,330 --> 00:01:35,910
because it leaves room for your heart.

41
00:01:36,300 --> 00:01:38,090
Now here's where the magic happens.

42
00:01:38,480 --> 00:01:40,070
At the end of every tiny branch,

43
00:01:40,370 --> 00:01:42,530
there's a bunch of air sacs, like grapes.

44
00:01:42,940 --> 00:01:44,180
They're called alveoli.

45
00:01:44,550 --> 00:01:47,120
And you've got around 480 million of them.

46
00:01:47,580 --> 00:01:50,220
Each one is wrapped in a net of tiny blood vessels.

47
00:01:50,630 --> 00:01:52,510
The wall between the air and your blood,

48
00:01:52,950 --> 00:01:55,710
is about 200 times thinner than a sheet of paper.

49
00:01:56,170 --> 00:01:58,730
So oxygen just slips across, into your blood.

50
00:01:59,120 --> 00:02:02,650
At the same time, carbon dioxide, your body's waste gas,

51
00:02:02,810 --> 00:02:04,730
slips the other way, into the air sac,

52
00:02:04,800 --> 00:02:06,160
ready to be breathed out.

53
00:02:06,590 --> 00:02:08,240
Spread all those sacs out flat,

54
00:02:08,690 --> 00:02:10,910
and they'd cover about 70 square meters.

55
00:02:11,380 --> 00:02:12,920
That's roughly a badminton court,

56
00:02:13,300 --> 00:02:14,870
folded up inside your chest.

57
00:02:15,280 --> 00:02:16,960
So who's in charge of all this?

58
00:02:17,450 --> 00:02:18,970
Not you, most of the time.

59
00:02:19,390 --> 00:02:22,670
A spot in your brainstem runs breathing on autopilot.

60
00:02:23,100 --> 00:02:24,380
And here's the surprise.

61
00:02:24,730 --> 00:02:26,730
It mostly isn't watching your oxygen.

62
00:02:27,080 --> 00:02:28,940
It's watching carbon dioxide.

63
00:02:29,290 --> 00:02:31,290
When CO2 builds up in your blood,

64
00:02:31,700 --> 00:02:34,470
your brainstem tells the diaphragm to breathe faster.

65
00:02:34,830 --> 00:02:37,220
That burning need to breathe when you hold your breath?

66
00:02:37,780 --> 00:02:41,840
That's mostly carbon dioxide piling up, not oxygen running out.

67
00:02:42,260 --> 00:02:46,490
In fact, the air you breathe out still has about 16 percent oxygen,

68
00:02:46,880 --> 00:02:48,890
compared to 21 percent going in.

69
00:02:49,270 --> 00:02:50,960
So your lungs aren't really pumps.

70
00:02:51,440 --> 00:02:54,110
They're a giant, folded-up trading floor,

71
00:02:54,210 --> 00:02:55,830
where air and blood swap gases,

72
00:02:56,200 --> 00:02:59,130
over 20,000 times a day, every day of your life.

73
00:02:59,600 --> 00:03:01,910
Next up, why can some animals see colors,

74
00:03:02,240 --> 00:03:03,370
we can't even imagine?

package.script: This shark drowns if you make it stop swimming. Wait, a fish that drowns? Sharks pull oxygen out of water as it flows over their gills. topic.title: Why don't woodpeckers get headaches?

package.title: Why Don't Woodpeckers Get Headaches at 20 Hits/Sec? 🐦
package.description:
Woodpeckers hammer trees up to 20 times a second, so why don't they get concussions? High-speed video from a 2022 study shows a woodpecker's head isn't a shock absorber at all: it's a stiff hammer, and its tiny brain is what keeps it safe.

Sources:
https://www.sci.news/biology/woodpecker-pecking-11004.html
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/woodpecker-skulls-dont-absorb-shock-like-previously-thought-180980426/

package.pinned_comment: If a woodpecker were as big as you, could it still peck? 🤔
package.script: Woodpecker pecks would concuss you. They do up to 20 a second, around 12,000 a day, and never get a headache. Why? For years, people said their skull was a shock absorber, like a built-in helmet. But in 2022, scientists filmed woodpeckers with high-speed cameras. And the head didn't cushion anything. The beak and the brain stopped together, like one stiff hammer. Which honestly makes sense. Nobody builds a hammer with a sponge inside. It would waste every swing. So the real secret is size. A woodpecker's brain is hundreds of times smaller than yours, and tiny brains can take much bigger jolts. That jolt that would knock you out? For them, it's well below the danger line. They'd have to hit twice as fast to get hurt. So if a woodpecker were as big as you, could it still peck?
key_facts: Woodpeckers can peck up to about 20 times a second and around 12,000 times a day
A 2022 Current Biology study (Van Wassenbergh et al.) filmed black, pileated and great spotted woodpeckers with high-speed cameras
The head does not absorb shock: beak and brain decelerate together, so the head acts as a stiff hammer
Each peck's deceleration exceeds the concussion threshold for humans, but small brains tolerate far bigger decelerations
Normal pecking stays well below a woodpecker's concussion threshold; they would need to hit about twice as fast to be at risk

topic.title: Why do apples float but potatoes sink?

package.title: Why Do Apples Float but Potatoes Sink? 🍎
package.description:
Why do apples float in water while potatoes sink? About a quarter of an apple is air trapped between its cells, so it's less dense than water, while a potato is packed with heavy starch grains.

Sources:
https://www.mashed.com/906273/the-real-reason-apples-float
https://www.freshplaza.com/north-america/article/2162560/why-do-apples-float

package.pinned_comment: What else in your kitchen do you think floats? 🍋🥚🍞
package.script: Your apple is twenty-five percent air. Your potato isn't. That's why one floats and one sinks. Drop both into a bowl of water. The apple bobs right back up. The potato heads straight for the bottom. The secret is density. Anything lighter than the same amount of water floats. Inside an apple, the cells aren't packed tightly. Between them are tiny pockets of air, about a quarter of the whole apple. So the apple ends up lighter than water, like a life jacket made of fruit. A potato is different. Its cells are stuffed with grains of starch, and starch is heavier than water. There's hardly any air in there, so down it goes. That's why bobbing for apples works. If apples sank, the game would be impossible! So what else in your kitchen is secretly full of air?
key_facts: About 25% of an apple's volume is air in pockets between its cells
That makes an apple less dense than water, so it floats
Potato cells are packed with starch grains; starch is denser than water
A potato's specific gravity is roughly 1.06-1.10, so it sinks

topic.title: Why does your voice sound so weird on a recording?

package.title: Only 38% Can Spot Their Own Voice on a Recording 🎙️
package.description:
Why does your voice sound so weird on a recording? When you talk, you hear yourself through the air and through the bones of your skull, which boosts the low tones, but a microphone only picks up the air part, so recordings sound higher and thinner than the voice in your head.

Sources:
https://wonderopolis.org/wonder/why-does-my-voice-sound-different-on-a-recording
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/09/130912112733.htm
https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Voice_confrontation

why do i hate my voice
package.pinned_comment: Be honest: would you recognize your own voice on a recording in 5 seconds? 🎙️
package.script: Only 38 percent of people knew their own voice on a recording. Your skull is why. That's a 1967 study, with five seconds to guess. When you talk, your vocal cords shake the air, and that sound curls around into your ears. But the buzz also takes a shortcut, straight through the bones of your skull. Your skull works like a built-in subwoofer. It boosts the deep tones, so you sound fuller and deeper to yourself. A microphone only catches the air part. No bones, no bass. So the recording sounds higher and thinner, and that's the voice everyone else hears. And in a 2013 study, people rated their own voice more attractive when they didn't know it was theirs. So your voice isn't bad, it's just unfamiliar. Be honest: would you have spotted your own voice?
key_facts: You hear your own voice through air conduction plus bone and tissue conduction; recordings capture only the air part
Bone and tissue conduction enhance lower frequencies, so your voice sounds fuller and deeper to you
In a 1967 study only 38% of people identified recordings of their own voice within 5 seconds
In a 2013 Albright College study of 80 people, participants rated their own voice more attractive when they didn't recognize it

package.pinned_comment: Which animal's eyes would you borrow for a day: the bee, the hummingbird or the mantis shrimp? 👀
package.script:
Hummingbirds see colors your brain has never made.
Not brighter colors, or sharper ones.
Whole new colors, with no names.
So how can an animal see a color we can't even imagine?
To find out, we have to start with you.
Light travels in waves of different lengths.
Your eyes catch a tiny slice of them,
from about 400 to 700 nanometers.
That slice is the rainbow,
violet at one end and red at the other.
Inside your eye are three kinds of color cells, called cones.
One likes blue light best, one likes green, and one likes red.
Every color you've ever seen,
is your brain comparing how hard those three are firing.
Yellow? That's your red and green cones firing together.
And here's a fun one.
Purple isn't in the rainbow at all.
When your red and blue cones fire, but green stays quiet,
your brain invents a color to fill the gap.
Scientists call that a non-spectral color.
Hold on to that idea.
Now take one cone away.
Dogs have just two, tuned to blue and yellow.
So a red ball on green grass,
looks to a dog like two similar, muddy shades.
Fewer cones, fewer colors.
So what happens with more?
Honeybees have three cones too, but they're shifted.
They see ultraviolet, blue and green.
Red? To a bee, red mostly looks dark.
Lots of flowers that look plain yellow to us,
have dark ultraviolet bullseyes in the middle.
They work like landing lights,
pointing the bee straight to the nectar.
Many birds go one step further.
They have four cone types, including one for ultraviolet.
Male and female blue tits look almost the same to us.
But in ultraviolet, the males' crowns shine brighter.
Now remember purple.
With three cones, you get one non-spectral color.
With four cones, there are way more ways to mix.
In 2020, scientists tested wild hummingbirds in the Rocky Mountains.
They lit up feeders with mixes like ultraviolet plus green.
And the birds learned to tell them apart from plain green.
That's a color you will never see.
It isn't greenish, or bluish.
It's something your brain has no slot for,
like trying to picture a brand new primary color.
So more cones always means more colors, right?
Meet the mantis shrimp.
It has around twelve kinds of color receptors.
For years, people said it must see a mind-blowing rainbow.
But in 2014, scientists actually tested it.
And it was worse than you at telling close shades apart.
Instead of comparing cones like we do,
it seems to read colors directly, like a barcode scanner.
Fast, but not fine.
So why bother seeing ultraviolet at all?
Take reindeer, out in the snowy Arctic.
Snow reflects ultraviolet, but their favorite food, lichen, soaks it up.
So scientists think lichen pops out as dark patches,
against the glowing snow.
Every animal sees the colors it needs to survive.
Your three cones are just one version of the world.
And somewhere, a hummingbird is looking at a flower,
in a color you'll never know.
Next up, what actually happens,
when a bee stings you?

Purple/magenta is a non-spectral color: the brain's mix of red and blue signals, not a single wavelength
Dogs have 2 cone types (blue and yellowish), so red and green look similar
Honeybees see ultraviolet, blue and green, and are not sensitive to red; many flowers have UV bullseye nectar guides
Many birds have 4 cone types including a UV/violet cone; blue tit males have more UV-reflective crowns
Stoddard et al. (Princeton, PNAS 2020) showed wild broad-tailed hummingbirds in the Rocky Mountains discriminate non-spectral colors such as UV+green
Mantis shrimp have about 12 color photoreceptor types but Thoen et al. (Science 2014) found poor discrimination of close colors; they appear to recognize colors directly
Reindeer eyes transmit UV; snow reflects UV while lichen absorbs it, so researchers think lichen stands out as dark

package.title: Why Can't Cats Taste Sugar? 1 Broken Gene 🐱
package.description:
Why can't cats taste sweet things? In 2005, scientists found that cats carry a broken copy of the Tas1r2 gene, one half of the sweet taste receptor, so sugar tastes like nothing to them, and lions, tigers and cheetahs share the same broken gene.

package.pinned_comment: Does your cat beg for ice cream, butter or yogurt? What do you think it's really after? 🐱
package.script: Your cat can't taste sugar, and one broken gene is why. Put a sweet treat in front of one, and to the cat, it tastes like nothing. To taste sweet, your tongue needs a tiny lock, built from two parts that work as a pair. In 2005, scientists looked inside cat DNA, and found one of those parts was broken. The gene for it is missing 247 letters, so the lock never gets built. No lock, no sweet. And it's not just house cats. Lions, tigers and cheetahs carry the same broken gene. Which honestly makes sense. Cats eat almost nothing but meat, and meat has barely any sugar. So losing sweet cost them nothing at all. So if your cat keeps stealing your ice cream, what do you think it's really after?
key_facts: Sweet taste needs a receptor made of two proteins, T1R2 and T1R3
Cats' Tas1r2 gene is a pseudogene missing 247 base pairs (Li et al., PLoS Genetics, 2005)

topic.title: Why do your feet grow before the rest of you?

package.title: Feet First, Torso Last: The 3-Step Teen Growth Spurt 🦶
package.description:
Why do your feet grow before the rest of your body? In the teen growth spurt, growth runs from the outside in: hands and feet first, then arms and legs, then the torso, and growth plates harden into solid bone around 13 to 17.

Sources:
https://healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/gradeschool/puberty/Pages/Physical-Development-Whats-Normal-Whats-Not.aspx

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: did your shoe size jump before you got taller? 🦶
package.script: Your feet grow before the rest of your body. It's why teenagers can look like baby giraffes. Big feet, long legs, and a body still catching up. So what's going on? Inside your bones are growth plates, soft strips of cartilage near each end. They keep adding new bone, until they harden into solid bone and close for good. When puberty kicks in, growth starts at the edges and works inward. Hands and feet go first, then your arms and legs, and your torso grows last. Small bones, like the ones in your fingers and toes, mature faster than the long bones in your legs. That's why teens trip over their own feet. Then, somewhere around 13 to 17, the last growth plates close, and the rest of you finally catches up. So, did your feet show up before the rest of you?

Growth plates are cartilage near bone ends that harden into solid bone; they usually close around 13-15 for girls and 15-17 for boys (KidsHealth)
Short bones like those in fingers and toes mature faster than long bones in the arms and legs (NIH/NICHD 2018)

topic.title: Why don't birds fly into each other in a flock?

package.title: Why Don't 10,000 Starlings Ever Crash? 🐦
package.description:
Why don't starlings crash into each other in a murmuration? Each bird tracks only about seven nearest neighbours, so a turn ripples through the flock as a wave that travels roughly three times faster than one bird can react.

Sources:
https://www.princeton.edu/news/2013/02/07/birds-feather-track-seven-neighbors-flock-together
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2234121
https://www.audubon.org/magazine/how-flock-birds-can-fly-and-move-together

Animated in the Pictogram Motion style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: Could you dodge a crowd of 10,000 people while watching just 7 of them? Who would your 7 be?
package.script: You'd crash in this flock, but ten thousand starlings never do. They swerve just inches apart, so why don't they slam into each other? There's no leader giving orders. Instead, each starling watches about seven neighbours. Close or far, it doesn't matter, it's always roughly seven. It copies their speed and their turns, and keeps a tiny gap. So when one bird turns, its seven neighbours turn too, then their neighbours, and the turn ripples through the flock like a wave. Scientists found that wave travels about three times faster than a single bird can react. Each bird sees it coming, like dancers in a chorus line. And seven seems to be the sweet spot, enough to stay together, without watching everyone at once. So could you dodge ten thousand people watching just seven?
key_facts: Each starling in a flock interacts with about 6-7 nearest neighbours regardless of distance (Ballerini et al., PNAS 2008; Young et al. 2013).
There is no leader; the flock's turns emerge from local copying of speed and direction.
Maneuver waves spread through flocks about three times faster than a single bird's reaction time, as birds anticipate the oncoming wave like a chorus line (Potts, Nature 1984).
Seven neighbours balances group cohesion against the effort of tracking others (Princeton, 2013).

package.script:
Why does a bee stinger keep pumping venom into you for up to seventy seconds,
after the bee flies away?
It's ripped out of her body, and it still works on its own.
So what actually happens in those few seconds after a sting?
Let's take it apart, one tiny piece at a time.
Part one. A saw that started as an egg tube.
Only female bees can sting.
That's because the stinger began as an egg-laying tube,
and male bees, called drones, don't have one at all.
Look closely and it isn't a needle.
It's three parts sliding together.
A central shaft called the stylet,
and two thin blades called lancets.
Each lancet is covered in backward-pointing barbs,
like the teeth on a tiny saw.
Part two. The stinger that walks itself in.
The two lancets slide up and down, one after the other.
One grips with its barbs, the other pushes deeper,
so the stinger actually walks itself into your skin.
And here's the wild part.
When the bee pulls away, the barbs hold tight,
and she leaves behind the whole pumping kit.
The venom sac, the muscles, and a little bundle of nerves.
In 2026, scientists filmed stingers in clear skin-like gel.
They saw a double piston pump.
Two pistons pushing in turns,
so venom only ever flows one way, into you.
The strong pumping kept going for fifteen to seventy seconds,
with no bee attached.
Part three. Why it hurts so much.
Up to half of dry bee venom is one ingredient, called melittin.
Melittin punches tiny holes in the cells it touches.
It also flips on your pain nerves and keeps them firing,
like someone leaning on a doorbell.
Then your body fights back.
It floods the spot with fluid from your blood to wash the venom away,
and that's the red, puffy bump you get.
Part four. Why the bee doesn't make it.
Your skin is thick and stretchy,
so those barbs can't slide back out.
When the bee flies off,
part of her belly tears away with the stinger.
She dies soon after.
But honeybees didn't evolve to sting us.
They usually fight other insects,
and a thin insect shell lets the stinger pull right out.
Wasps and bumblebees have smoother stingers,
so they can sting again and again.
Part five. A sting that calls for backup.
A sting also releases an alarm scent,
and it smells a lot like bananas.
To other bees, that smell means one thing.
Danger, right here.
It tags you as the target, so more bees can find you.
That's why bees act like a team.
One worker gives up her life,
and the whole hive stays protected.
And here's what scientists found about that leftover stinger.
Scraping it off or pinching it out works about the same.
What matters is speed.
Every second it stays in, it pumps a little more.
Next time, find out why your stomach is full of acid strong enough to eat through some metals,
and still doesn't digest itself.

The stinger is a central stylet plus two barbed lancets that slide alternately and drive it deeper
A detached honeybee stinger keeps pumping: UNSW (Oct 2026) filmed strong regular pumping for 15-70 seconds, via a double-piston pump
Melittin is about 40-60% of dry honeybee venom; it forms pores in cells and activates pain receptors
Redness and swelling come from fluid released from the blood to flush the venom
Barbs catch in thick mammal skin, so the honeybee's abdomen ruptures and she dies; she can usually sting insects and pull free
Wasps and bumblebees have smooth stingers and can sting repeatedly
The alarm pheromone (isoamyl acetate) smells like bananas and recruits other bees
Scraping vs pinching makes no real difference; removing the stinger quickly is what matters

package.description:

package.script: Lose your eyebrows and 54% of people can't name your face. MIT scientists tested it in 2003. They showed people famous faces with the eyes erased, and they still named sixty percent. But erase just the eyebrows, and it dropped to forty-six. So why do we even have them? Picture sweat rolling down your forehead. Your brow bone and that arch catch it like a gutter, and the hairs all point out toward your ears, so the drops slide off to the sides, and not into your eyes. Rain too. Each brow has about 250 hairs on the job. But their biggest job? Talking without words. One brow up means, really? Both up means surprise! Pulled down and together? Somebody's grumpy. So can you raise just one eyebrow? Left, right, or neither?

Frogs actually swallow with their eyeballs.
You've just never noticed why.
Watch a frog gulp down a cricket,
and its eyes squeeze shut
and sink right into its head.
That's not a blink.
A frog's eye sockets are open underneath,
with no solid bone floor.
So muscles yank each eyeball down,
into the roof of its mouth.
Now those eyes press on the bug like two thumbs,
shoving it back toward the throat.
Why bother?
Frogs don't chew.
Their tiny teeth only grip,
so dinner goes down whole.

With those eye muscles switched off,
each cricket took 74 percent more swallows.
About four gulps instead of two.
So a frog's eyes spot the bug,
then help push it down.
Next time a frog blinks at you,
is it winking,
or eating?

package.script: How do kangaroos hit 50 kilometres an hour with almost no extra energy, when you'd be gasping? As a red kangaroo hops faster, its oxygen use barely changes. So why hop instead of run? package.title: Why Doesn't Your Stomach Digest Itself?
package.description:
Your stomach is full of hydrochloric acid strong enough to dissolve zinc, so why doesn't it digest itself? Your stomach explained in simple words: parietal cells and pepsin, the bicarbonate mucus shield, tight junctions, and a lining that replaces itself every few days.

package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think stomach acid could actually dissolve metal? 🧪
package.script: Your stomach is full of acid strong enough to dissolve metal. So why doesn't it dissolve you? The secret is a wall that rebuilds itself every few days. Every day it breaks down steak, cheese and crunchy vegetables, but it never eats the walls holding it all in. For a long time, nobody knew what a stomach actually did. Some thought it just ground food up like a mill. Then in the 1700s, an Italian scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani pulled stomach juice out on a sponge tied to a string. And he showed that this juice could dissolve meat even outside the body. So the stomach wasn't just a grinder. It was a chemistry lab. And later, the French scientist Claude Bernard noticed something odd. The stomach wall acts as if it were made of porcelain. So what's inside this lab? Your stomach lining is covered in millions of tiny pits. Deep down in them, special cells called parietal cells pump out hydrochloric acid. That gives your stomach juice a pH of about one and a half to three and a half. At its strongest, it's even more acidic than lemon juice. Strong enough to dissolve a piece of zinc. Next door, chief cells make an enzyme called pepsin, which chops proteins into little pieces. And here's the clever part. Pepsin is made switched off. It leaves the cell as a harmless version called pepsinogen, and only the acid outside can switch it on. So the knife is never sharp inside the cell that makes it. But that still leaves the stomach wall sitting in acid. That's where defense number one comes in: slime. The lining is coated in a thick, sticky layer of mucus. And that mucus is loaded with bicarbonate, the same kind of stuff as baking soda. Acid trickles in from one side, bicarbonate soaks it up from the other. In lab studies, the acid on one side of the mucus was strong, but right against the cells, it was close to neutral. Under the slime, the cells are zipped together with tight junctions, so acid can't leak between them. Defense number two is even wilder. Your stomach just keeps replacing itself. The surface lining is completely renewed every three to six days. One old estimate says about half a million cells get shed every minute. So even if a few cells get burned, fresh ones are already on the way. And this stomach is built to stretch. Empty, it's about the size of your fist. But it can hold up to four liters, more than seventy-five times its empty size. Every twenty seconds or so, a wave of muscle squeezes the mix, and two to four hours after a meal, it's pushed on into your gut. So what can break the shield? package.script:
Your window kills birds,
and they never see it coming. But why?
To a bird, your window is just more sky.
Clear glass lets a bird look straight through,
right at the plants inside.
Or the glass acts like a mirror,
showing trees and clouds behind it.
Either way, it sees an open path,
and flies full speed into a wall it never saw.
Nothing in nature is solid and see-through,
so birds never learned to expect it.
In the US,
scientists think windows kill up to a billion birds a year.
So what actually helps?
One hawk sticker barely helps.
The bird just flies around it.
But dots spaced about two inches apart
look like a fence,
so the bird turns away.
Next time you hear a thump,
go look at your window from outside.
What does a bird see in it?

package.script:
Why does your arm hair stop growing,
but your head hair keeps going for years?
Every hair grows from a tiny pocket in your skin
called a follicle.
And every follicle runs on a loop.
Grow. Stop. Rest. Fall out.
Then a new hair starts in the same spot.
The trick is how long the growing part lasts.
On your head, it can run two to seven years.
At about a centimeter a month,
that's long enough to reach your waist.
On your arms, it lasts just a few months.
So the hair hits its limit,
and falls out before it ever gets long.
Arm hair doesn't grow slower.
It just quits way sooner.
Your eyebrows have a short timer too.
So if your arm hair had a seven year timer,
how long would you let it grow?

Hair grows roughly half an inch (about 1 to 1.25 cm) a month, a commonly cited dermatology figure

package.script:
A toucan's beak is secretly a radiator.
Here's why you never noticed.
That giant bill is a third of the bird's length,
but barely a twentieth of its weight.
It's mostly air.
Thin sheets of keratin, the stuff in your nails,
wrap a foam of tiny bone struts.
Now the clever part.
Under that shell runs a web of blood vessels.
When the toucan gets hot,
it pumps warm blood into the beak,
and the heat pours out into the air.
Scientists filmed it with a heat camera
and watched the beak light up.
When it's chilly, it shuts the flow off
and keeps that heat inside.
For short bursts,
almost all the heat it loses
goes out through that beak.
Be honest, would you trade your nose
for a radiator on your face?

package.pinned_comment: Are you the one dripping at the gym or the one who barely sweats? 💧
package.script:
You have up to four million sweat glands.
So why do some people drip,
while others barely look damp?
Picture two people, same hot room, same workout.
One is soaked. The other is fine.
It's not about being healthy or unhealthy.
It comes down to your body's cooling system,
and how hard it's been trained.
Let's start with the hardware.
Your skin is packed with two to four million sweat glands.
Each one is a tiny coiled tube,
buried in your skin like a curly straw.
They cover almost your whole body,
with the most on your palms, the soles of your feet,
and your forehead.
Now here's how they switch on.
Deep in your brain sits a thermostat called the hypothalamus.
When your core gets even slightly too warm,
it fires a signal down your nerves.
The glands squeeze out salty water onto your skin.
And then comes the clever part.
Sweat doesn't cool you by being wet.
It cools you by disappearing.
When it evaporates, it carries heat away with it.
That's why a humid day feels so awful.
The air is already full of water,
so your sweat just sits there and drips.
And fresh sweat barely smells at all.
The smell comes from bacteria
munching on sweat from your armpit glands.
So why does one person drip while another stays dry?
First, size.
A bigger body makes more heat when it moves,
so it needs more sweat to dump it.
Second, your genes.
Some people simply have more active glands,
or glands that pump harder.
Third, men and women tend to differ.
In a study in Japan,
fit men started sweating fastest of everyone,
and inactive women sweated the least.
But here's the twist most people get backwards.
Sweating a lot usually means you're fitter, not less fit.
A trained body is like an upgraded air conditioner.
It turns on sooner,
before you even feel hot,
and it pumps out more sweat once it gets going.
Heat training does the same thing.
Spend around one to two weeks exercising in the heat,
and your body starts sweating earlier,
pours out more,
and holds on to more of its salt.
Now let's talk numbers.

package.title: An Egg Holds 3 kg, So How Does a Chick Get Out? 🐣
package.description:
Why doesn't an egg crack when a hen sits on it? The egg's dome shape spreads outside pressure across the whole shell, so an egg squeezed end to end can hold about 3 kg, while a chick pecking one spot from the inside, and pulling calcium from the shell as it grows, breaks out easily.

package.script:
A hen sits on her eggs for 21 days,
and they don't crack.
So how does a tiny chick break out?
It's all about the shape.
An egg is a dome, like a stone arch.
Push on the outside,
and the force spreads across the whole shell,
so no single spot takes the load.
Squeezed end to end,
an egg can hold about three kilos.
Plus the hen's weight is shared by the nest and the other eggs.
From the inside, it's a different story.
The chick pecks one tiny spot,
and a dome is weak against a push from inside.
Here's the clever part.
The chick pulls calcium from the shell to build its bones,
so the shell gets thinner as it grows.
Strong outside, weak inside.
So could you crack an egg squeezing it end to end?

topic.title: How does a snail crawl on just one foot?

package.title: How Does a Snail Move on Just 1 Foot? 🐌
package.description:
How do snails move on one foot? Waves of muscle ripple along a snail's foot while its slime acts as glue under the still parts and turns runny where a wave pushes, so the snail slides forward at roughly a millimetre a second.

Sources:

package.script:
A snail never lifts its one foot.
Can you guess how it moves?
Put a snail on glass and look underneath.
Dark stripes ripple along the sole,
from the tail toward the head.
Those are waves of muscle,
squeezing and stretching the foot.
But the real trick is the slime.
Under the still parts of the foot,
it's thick and sticky, like glue.
Where a wave pushes on it,
it turns runny and slippery.
So each wave slides forward on liquid,
while the rest stays stuck down.
Glue, slide, glue, slide.
That grip lets a snail climb straight up a stem,
or hang under a leaf.
The catch? It's slow.
Roughly one millimetre a second.
So would you trade your two feet
for one slimy one?

Pedal mucus acts as a glue for adhesion, and shear-thins to flow where a wave passes, then re-gels (Denny 1980, Nature; ScienceInsights)
Adhesion lets snails resist gravity on plants (Denny 1980)
A common garden snail moves roughly 1 mm per second (ScienceInsights; sources vary)

package.title: Why Do Worms Come Out When It Rains? 2 Theories 🪱
package.description:
Why do earthworms come out when it rains if they don't drown? Worms breathe through their wet skin and can survive days underwater, so scientists think rain vibrations or an easy chance to travel far on wet ground bring them up.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-earthworms-surface-after-rain/
https://blog.nature.org/2019/04/15/the-real-reason-you-see-earthworms-after-rain

package.script:
That worm on your sidewalk isn't drowning.
So why did it crawl out?
We're told rain floods their tunnels.
But a worm doesn't have lungs.
It breathes through its skin,
and that skin has to stay wet.
Scientists have kept worms underwater for days,
and they just keep wiggling.
So what's going on?
One idea is drumming.
Raindrops tap the ground like a digging mole,
and worms escape moles by heading up.
But lots of experts doubt it.
The favorite theory is simpler.
Underground, a worm squeezes through dirt bit by bit.
On wet ground it slides fast and far,
to find food, a new home, or a mate.
Dry ground would dry out its skin,
so rain is the perfect chance.
Basically, a worm highway.
So next time you spot one,
is it escaping a flood,
or going on a road trip?
key_facts: Earthworms have no lungs and breathe through their skin, which must stay moist (Scientific American, Earthworm Society)
Earthworms can survive several days fully submerged; many species two weeks or more (Scientific American; The Nature Conservancy)
